--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.subgraph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Extract an induced subgraph containing the specified nodes. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.subgraph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Extract an induced subgraph containing the specified nodes. title: >- [Graph.subgraph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Extract an induced subgraph containing the specified nodes. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Extract an induced subgraph containing the specified nodes. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L55387-L55493){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.subgraph(nodes) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Induced subgraph](../assets/graphs/subgraph.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A six-node graph with node ids 1 to 6; nodes 1, 2, 4, 5 are the ones requested. The induced subgraph keeps those four nodes and every edge among them (1-2, 1-4, 2-5, 4-5), in the accent color; nodes 3 and 6 and their edges are dropped and shown dashed." width="100%"} Returns a new graph containing only the specified nodes and all edges between them (the induced subgraph). This is a direct method that doesn't require prior selection, unlike `transform_to_subgraph_ws()`. An edge is kept only when both of its endpoints are among the requested nodes, so any edge leading out of the chosen set is dropped. Use it to zoom in on a region of a larger network: - analyzing one community, module, or connected component on its own - extracting the neighborhood of a node of interest for closer inspection or plotting - running an expensive algorithm on a manageable piece of a large graph The original graph is not modified. Nodes and edges keep their IDs, so results computed on the subgraph can be matched back to the original by ID. The selection state is not carried over. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [nodes]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of node IDs to include in the subgraph. Order does not matter, and repeated IDs are included once. An empty list gives an empty graph. To work from labels, convert them first with `get_id_from_label()`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : New graph containing only the specified nodes and edges between them. Preserves directedness, weightedness, and node and edge IDs, labels, weights and attributes. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If any node ID is not found in the graph. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~edge_subgraph`) : Extract specific edges and their endpoints. [](`~transform_to_subgraph_ws`) : Extract the subgraph defined by the current selection. ## Examples {.doc-examples} The subgraph on a set of nodes keeps every edge between them and drops the rest. The nodes keep their IDs, labels and attributes. `C` has ID `3` in both graphs, and the edges to `B` are gone: ::: {#fa414f13 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(weighted=True).add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) g.add_edges([("A", "B", 1.0), ("B", "C", 2.0), ("C", "D", 3.0)]) g.add_edge("A", "C", weight=4.0) ids = [g.get_id_from_label(label) for label in ["A", "C", "D"]] sub = g.subgraph(ids) sub.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True), sub.get_id_from_label("C") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (['C--D', 'A--C'], 3) ``` ::: ::: ### The chess club `ec.friends()` is a network of friendships among the 24 members of a chess club and a climbing club. The subgraph on the 12 chess players keeps the 20 friendships among them and drops their ties to climbers. Here the subgraph is highlighted in the whole network: ::: {#4d72b701 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} friends = ec.friends() nodes = friends.get_node_df() chess_ids = nodes.filter(club="Chess")["id"].to_list() chess = friends.subgraph(chess_ids) chess.count_nodes(), chess.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (12, 20) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#856a3d8f .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} friends.plot( label_by="label", highlight=chess_ids, seed=3, highlight_edges=[(s, t) for _, s, t in chess.get_edges_as_tuples()], ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: On its own, the chess club is a group of six on the left and one of five on the right, joined by Femi and Gwen at the top and by Hugo at the bottom: ::: {#19d4b909 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} chess.plot(label_by="label", seed=1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: `subgraph()` takes node IDs. To keep the edges, rather than the nodes, use `edge_subgraph()`. [Transforming graphs](../user-guide/transforming.qmd#subgraphs) extracts the strongest ties of *Les Misérables*, and explains how a subgraph keeps its IDs.
